title: Infra Playbook: GPU Fleet Capacity, Terraform IaC, CI/CD, and Runbooks
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary

This playbook consolidates operational guidance, standards, and runbooks for Redwood's infrastructure teams related to the GPU fleet and capacity planning, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, networking and cloud accounts, and high-priority runbooks. The document is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, operating, and scaling inference capacity.

Scope

- GPU fleet and capacity planning for hosted and dedicated environments
- Terraform modules, state management, and module lifecycle
- CI/CD pipelines and build artifacts for infra components and runtime images
- Cloud accounts, VPC design, and networking connectivity patterns for GPUs
- Runbooks for common operational incidents (capacity shortage, OOMs, node failures)
- Team onboarding links and troubleshooting references

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: infra-platform (engineering)
- Escalation: oncall-infra@redwood.com (primary rotation)
- Pager: SRE rotation (pager duty)
- Service owners: GPU Fleet (team: serving-runtime), Network (team: eng-infra-networking), Terraform modules (team: infra-iac)

Key SLAs and SLOs

| Metric | Target | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 95th perc. request latency for provisioning (scale-up) | < 60s | > 90s for 5m | infra-platform |
| Node availability (GPU nodes) | 99.9% | < 99.7% 1h | eng-sre |
| Average GPU utilization (prod cluster) | 30-60% | > 80% or < 15% sustained 1h | GPU Fleet |
| Terraform plan drift detection | 0 drift | any drift on prod | infra-iac |

GPU Fleet and Capacity Planning

Overview

- Fleet model: mixed instance pools (on-demand reserved for Dedicated, spot-backed for burst) across us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1.
- Node types: a100-80gb (training-compatible), a10g / h100 variants for inference, plus cpu-only bootstrap nodes.
- Autoscaling policy: multi-dimensional autoscaler considering queued requests, per-node token throughput, and model KV cache hit ratios.

Capacity forecasting process (monthly)

1. Export token consumption and model mix from telemetry for last 90 days.
2. Project growth using 3 growth scenarios (p50: +15%/mo, p75: +30%/mo, p95: +60%/mo).
3. Translate token demand to GPU-hours using per-model perf profile (tokens/sec per GPU) from model catalog.
4. Validate headroom: ensure 48-72 hours of burst capacity available for top 10 customer workloads.
5. Publish capacity runbook update and open capacity planning PR in infra-roadmap.

Tagging and naming conventions

- All GPU instances must include tags: service=gpu-fleet, env=prod|staging|dev, owner=@team, model-family= (e.g., llama2, gptx).
- KMS key: alias/redwood/infra/gpu-state for encrypted volumes and secrets.

Cost controls and reservation guidance

- Dedicated pools: use reserved instances / capacity reservations for top 3 enterprise customers.
- Spot usage cap: max 40% for steady-state inference; set fallback policies to on-demand pool.
- Batching and cache tuning to reduce per-token GPU time are primary cost levers.

Cloud Accounts and Networking

VPC layout and peering

- Per-environment VPCs: redwood-prod-vpc, redwood-staging-vpc, redwood-dev-vpc.
- Subnets: public (bastion, load balancers), private (GPU nodes, control-plane), management (CI runners, image repo access).
- Transit/peering: use AWS Transit Gateway for cross-region connectivity for control-plane replication; avoid full-mesh peering.

Network security controls

- Security groups: minimal open ports; GPU nodes accept inbound only from control-plane LB and monitoring ranges.
- IP restrictions: restrict management plane to corporate CIDR and SSO-enabled jump hosts.
- NAT and egress: image pulls go through centralized image proxy for auditing.

IAM and principle of least privilege

- Cloud accounts are grouped into org units: infra-prod, infra-sec, infra-dev.
- Use IAM roles for service accounts; no long-lived IAM user credentials in Terraform state.
- Approval process for elevated network changes: design review + security signoff + one-week staged rollout.

Terraform / Infrastructure as Code Modules

Repository layout and module standards

- repo: infrastructure/modules (public modules shared across teams)
- Each high-level module must include: README.md, inputs.tf, outputs.tf, examples/, CHANGELOG.md, and a module-wide tests/ directory with terratest/integration tests.
- Module versioning: semver (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Only bump MAJOR for breaking changes; deprecate old module versions with 90-day notice.

State management and locking

- Backend: S3 + DynamoDB for locking (prod bucket: redwood-terraform-state-prod).
- State key conventions: env/component/region.tfstate (e.g., prod/gpu-fleet/us-west-2.tfstate).
- IAM for state access: limited to infra-iac and CI system role.

Example backend config (reference):

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "redwood-terraform-state-prod"
    key            = "prod/gpu-fleet/us-west-2.tfstate"
    region         = "us-west-2"
    dynamodb_table = "redwood-terraform-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
```

Module publishing and releases

- Publish module versions by tagging repo and publishing a release (automated via CI).
- Automated security scans (tfsec, checkov) and policy checks (OPA) are required before merging to main.
- Any manual infra change in prod requires: design PR -> tf plan run in staging -> security review -> 24h canary -> prod apply window.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Pipeline patterns

- IaC pipelines: PR -> plan (preview) in CI (using ephemeral plan viewer) -> approvals -> apply via CI role with short-lived creds.
- Image pipelines: build runtime images in build cluster, sign and publish to internal registry (registry.redwood.com/gpu-runtime:<sha>).
- Release gating: smoke test set (small model + inference) must pass on canary cluster before global rollout.

Key pipeline checks

- Linting: terraform fmt, tfsec, checkov
- Tests: terratest infra integration, unit tests for helper scripts
- Secrets: use Vault + CI OIDC to fetch short-lived credentials during apply

Example pipeline snippet (conceptual):

1. PR created -> CI runs fmt/lint/tests
2. CI posts terraform plan to PR with resource delta
3. Reviewer approves -> maintainer triggers apply job in protected pipeline (requires 2 approvers for prod)
4. Canary window: apply to canary workspace, run health checks (10m), then apply staged rollout to remaining workspaces

Runbooks (High priority)

A. Capacity shortage (sustained high queued requests)

1. Pager triggers: queued_requests > 1000 for 5m or provisioning latency > 90s (alerting rule infra/capacity-high).
2. Triage steps:
   a. Check autoscaler logs: kubectl -n infra logs deploy/autoscaler | tail -n 200
   b. Verify spot fallback: aws autoscaling describe-policies --auto-scaling-group-name gpu-spot-asg
   c. Manually scale Dedicated pool if autoscale stuck: terraform apply -var='dedicated_pool_size=...' (use protected pipeline).
   d. If immediate relief required, enable burst-on-demand policy via console flag: /infra/ops/flags -> enable burst_force_on_demand.
3. Post-incident: run root-cause analysis, update capacity forecast, and create a postmortem in confluence under incident reviews.

B. GPU OOMs / Model crashes

1. Symptoms: pods restarting, nginx 502s to inference endpoints for a model family.
2. Steps:
   a. Check pod logs and OOMKilled: kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide; kubectl logs <pod> --previous
   b. Check model KV cache size and per-request token limit; temporarily limit request token size via rate-limiter: config route -> max_tokens=1024
   c. Roll back to previous model variant with lower memory if recent rollout caused instability.

C. Node unreachable / hardware failure

1. Detect: node NotReady or unreachable from control-plane.
2. Steps:
   a. Remove node from load balancer and cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
   b. Check node-level metrics and try soft-reboot via cloud API (aws ec2 reboot-instances --instance-ids i-...)
   c. If hardware fault, trigger replacement workflow: infra-ticket to HW replacement and provision new node from spare pool.

Team Wiki and Onboarding

- How to get access: request infra-iac access via SSO groups (infra-iac-dev / infra-iac-prod) and complete IaC security training.
- Local dev flow: use terraform workspace "dev-<yourname>", run plan with: terraform plan -var-file=dev.tfvars -refresh=false.
- Testing modules: refer to infrastructure/modules/<module>/tests/ for terratest examples.

Change and Release Process

- All infra changes follow: RFC (if design changes) -> PR -> CI plan -> security scans -> 2 approvers -> staged rollout.
- Emergency changes: tagged as emergency in PR and require post-facto review within 24 hours.

Appendices

A. Useful commands

- View terraform state list: aws s3 ls s3://redwood-terraform-state-prod/prod/gpu-fleet/
- Review autoscaler health: kubectl -n infra get deployment autoscaler -o yaml
- Rebuild runtime image: make build-runtime IMAGE=registry.redwood.com/gpu-runtime:<sha>

B. Links and references

- Model performance catalog: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- GPU runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Terraform guide: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026
